newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya approves issuance of corporate bonds.
newsitem.headline: Kenya approves issuance of corporate bonds.

text.p: Kenya's capital markets bodies have approved the listing and trading of corporate bonds on the Nairobi Stock Exchange which they hope will help bring down runaway interest rates, Nairobi's bourse chief said on Tuesday.

"Because corporate bonds reduce financial intermediation, demand for bank advances should decline and in turn trigger a drop in interest rates," Nairobi Stock Exchange (NSE) Chairman Jimnah Mbaru said in a statement issued in the capital Nairobi.
"Such bonds will be listed and traded on the exchange. This will provide a secondary market...they will be bought and sold through brokers just like the shares," Mbaru added.
Mbaru, one of Kenya's leading lights in market reforms, said trading in corporate bonds marked the introduction of the most important (trading) instrument in Kenya's economic development.
Kenyan interest rates on government treasury bills are at around 18-25 percent while commercial bank lending rates are in the 24-33 percent range.

Mbaru said the corporate bond market was estimated at 30 billion shillings ($535.7 million) and issuance of the bonds was a big relief to companies that needed long-term funds for expansion, modernisation or working capital requirements.
"At the moment, there are 58 equities and 13 preference shares (on the Nairobi Stock Exchange). Preference shares are rarely traded. There is need for more instruments," he said.

Mbaru said the regulatory body Capital Markets Authority's (CMA) approval fee would be 0.1 percent -- low enough to encourage the market. The first 50 million shillings would attract a commission of a sixteenth percent while funds above 50 million shillings would tap a twentieth percent commission.
Issuance of corporate bonds will be open to companies listed or not listed on the Nairobi bourse but they must meet listing requirements and have a good (operating) track record, he said.

He gave among listing requirements as minimum debt raised not being less than 20 million shillings, submitting a prospectus to the CMA and Nairobi Stock Exchange and securities for which listing was sought being freely transferable.

The primary market price of a bond will be pegged on the treasury bills rate. While the rate will serve as the floor price, the actual price will be two-three percentage points above, depending on the quality of the company, Mbaru said.
"Fluctuations in market rates is the single most important factor in determining the value of a bond. If interest rates rise after an issue, the value of the bond goes down," he said.

Kenya has implemented a range of economic changes on the bourse in the last few years, including allowing foreign investment. The government has pledged to sell treasury bills on the bourse secondary market -- expected sometime next year.
The Nairobi Stock Exchange is capitalised at around $1.89 billion.
